metadata.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warns of AI concentration risks

content.text:
In an interview with the Wall Street Journal, Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Satya Nadella warned of the growing concentration in the handful of artificial intelligence companies leading the AI boom.
Morning Brief Host Julie Hyman and Semafor business and finance editor Liz Hoffman break down where Nadella's biggest concerns lie.
Private developers Anthropic (ANTH.PVT) and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) are set for mega-IPOs in late 2026, with Microsoft owning 27% of the latter's for-profit arm.
Satya Nadella gave an interview to the Wall Street Journal. I I got to say I'm a little confused about what's going on with Nadella here. You know, he he basically is criticizing frontier models, that is Open AI, Anthropic as being um having too much power, seems to be what he's talking about. And I know that like sort of Microsoft is decoupling a little bit from Open AI, but also like they're still very intertwined with them.
Satya is obviously talking his own book here, right? I think if you look at where they thought they would be now, um with respect to what they're doing internally, what their partners are doing, where they are in AI, it has changed like dramatically and I think they they probably feel like they're a bit behind. But you know, he had this blog post out or an ex post out a week ago and honestly I had to read it like four or five times. I was like, what is going on here? And I think ultimately the point he's making, it is um again, in his interest to do it. It's where Microsoft has placed the bet, which is that they don't have their own frontier model. His view is that companies ought to be able to unplug from Open AI and plug into anthropic without losing any of that institutional knowledge and that that's really on companies um to kind of create that what he saw say learning loops, compounding intelligence. Um and obviously Microsoft wants to be the ecosystem in which that happens. Um right? They they have sort of made the bet that frontier models are all going to kind of converge. There's going to be one or two winners, maybe one direct consumer winner, one enterprise winner, but that you're boiling the same ocean and so ultimately you're going to end up kind of with the same intelligence that actually the value is on how end customers use it and Microsoft wants to be sort of the lab that that happens in.
Yeah, I mean, I don't necessarily disagree, but at the same time if I think that the train has already left the station in some ways, right? Uh especially if you look at all of the partnerships that that Anthropic has done with enterprise customers, it it seems like that's not companies are not necessarily going to be able to unplug and plug in elsewhere and that that already it might be too late perhaps to make that argument.
I think about it kind of like Uber and Lyft. Like you take out your phone and you're like, but there was never a layer that sat on top of them that said actually pick this one. And and I don't know whether um AI will systems will come up with a, you know, here's the right model for the thing you're trying to do, kind of price agnostic, whatever whatever it might be. No one has sat there yet, but I think the question for the the frontier labs is, are they a bigger threat to the players one step above them, the Microsoft who obviously is feeling the heat, that's where these kind of messages come from. Or the or the step below them, the law firms, design firms, architects, whatever, right? Like, you know, I think every question, the question that every uh startup founder out there raising money right now is getting is when is Open AI and anthropic going to decide to do what you do and and how long a head start do you have? So I I think there there's tension in both directions. I don't have a great sense of which way the labs would like to eat themselves out of that out of that first, but they clearly have huge power and huge ambitions and that makes people like Satya really nervous.
